metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. In the chosen experimental design, TTB and Tallying make diametrically opposed predictions on 5 out of the 6 trial types, and on the 6th trial TTB makes a deterministic prediction while Tallying predicts a tie. Consequently, data generated by the TTB model will yield a metric value close to 1.0 (modulo response noise), whereas data generated by Tallying will yield a metric value close to 0.0 (as it consistently chooses the opposite option). This creates a massive, easily detectable gap between the two theories.

The experimental design contains specific trials where Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) make strictly opposite predictions. For example, when option A has the single highest validity cue but option B has a greater number of lower validity cues. This metric isolates only those discriminating trials and calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic. For data generated by Tallying, this proportion will be close to 1 (modulo noise), whereas for data generated by TTB, it will be close to 0. This creates a maximal and highly stable contrast between the two theories.

This metric calculates the choice probability of the option [1, 0, 1, 0, 0] over [0, 1, 0, 1, 0] (Trial 2). Under Tallying, both options win on exactly 2 features, leading to an indifferent 50% choice probability regardless of the beta and epsilon parameters. Under the WADD model, the option [1, 0, 1, 0, 0] strictly dominates because its winning features (validities 0.95 and 0.6) are strictly more valid than the opponent's winning features (validities 0.9 and 0.55). Thus, WADD will consistently predict a choice probability > 50% for the target option.

This metric isolates trials where the two theories make maximally divergent predictions (Trials 1 and 3). In these trials, one option has more positive features overall (favored by Tallying), but the other option possesses the fewer, highest-validity features (favored by WADD). Tallying will consistently choose the option with the higher unweighted sum, whereas WADD will penalize it for lacking the top features and choose the other option. By calculating the proportion of times the subject chooses the option with the higher unweighted sum in these specific trials, we expect a value close to 1.0 for Tallying and close to 0.0 for WADD, cleanly discriminating the two models.
